_: The core user units, one row each. THE only list: install.sh links and enables from it, cc-audit checks health from it, cc-land reads its restart policy from it, and tests/check.sh fails when a unit file and this file disagree. Adding a timer = its two unit files + one row here.

_fields.enable: required = install.sh enables it and cc-audit FAILS when it is not enabled · owner = linked only, the box owner switches it on, and cc-audit checks its health only once they have · timer = started by its own .timer, never enabled and never health-checked
_fields.start: what install.sh does after enabling: now = --now · no-block = start --no-block (a oneshot that may wait minutes for the network must never block the installer) · none
_fields.health: active = systemctl is-active must say active · not-failed = a oneshot that has run and gone idle, only is-failed is a fault · none
_fields.restart: what a landing does when this unit's file, or a file its ExecStart runs, changes: restart = restart it · rearm = restart it AND confirm list-timers shows a next trigger (daemon-reload alone leaves a changed OnCalendar with Trigger: n/a — a daily job silently switched off, 2026-08-31) · owner = never automatically: the landing ASKS the owner instead, once per unit — the unit and the command on its card, and a row in the ask ledger that stays open until somebody restarts it, so a second landing on the same unit says nothing again (three landings changed one such unit's code and nobody was ever told, 2026-09-08 to 2026-09-11) · none = nothing to restart, the next start picks the change up
_fields._daemons: the `daemons` array below is the same declaration for a long-lived process this tree starts OUTSIDE systemd — one systemctl knows nothing about, which is how a landing restarted every unit it touched and still left a server on the pre-merge code while reporting success (2026-09-07). Its fields: `daemon` a name · `runs` the file the process is running, which is how it is RECOGNISED among this user's processes · `paths` the files that make it out of date (default: just `runs`) · `restart` the argv that brings it back, whose first token is a path in this tree and the rest literal arguments, or `owner` = named and never restarted from a landing, or `none` = the next start picks it up. A process no row here declares is never restarted by a landing — it is NAMED in the deploy's own output and left running.
_fields.paths: optional: the files and directories this unit RUNS, relative to this tree — for a unit whose ExecStart names one entry point over a whole package, where an ExecStart-basename test sees nothing move (a merged dashboard sat on the previous version's process for want of this, 2026-09-06). A box that keeps this tree as core/ inside a private overlay declares its own units the same way, in the overlay's config/units.json

units.why: owns the shared tmux server every session on this box lives in — restarting it takes all of them down, so it is the owner's hand (`cc rc restart`)
the 10 s alive timestamp that dates a power loss
a boot oneshot: restarting it would re-announce a boot that already happened
the 60 s model-fallback tick: switched off, a usage limit stops every loop on the box

the 60 s flush of the event broker: a finding or a nag it deduped is held until its debounce is up, and this is what hands the digest over. Switched off, a held event waits for the next thing that happens to wake that session — and a delivery nobody took is never retried

the steward's own tick, every 30 min. cc-broker.timer delivers events; this one carries the LEDGER — the lines a repeat writes, which wake nobody by design and ride out only on that target's next real message, so a quiet target leaves them in a file no turn opens. Enabled everywhere and still free: with CC_STEWARD_SOURCES unset in ~/.cc/config every run exits without calling anything, and that one key is the whole switch. Switched off, nothing reads a ledger line until something else happens to wake that session

the 60 s inbox drain: a message that arrived while a session's pane was busy or holding a dialog is spooled, and this is what hands it over once the pane is free. Switched off, every such message waits for the next thing that happens to type at that session — which on 2026-09-01 was hours

the 2 min dialog sweep: cc-msg's known-safe table at every pane on the box, paused or not. cc-msg.timer answers a dialog only on its way to delivering a message, so a session nobody writes to kept its dialog for as long as nobody did — six of them, hours, 2026-09-10. Switched off, a modal at a pane with nothing queued behind it stands until a person presses it

the board-against-the-box reconciliation, and the three riders its service names: cc-handoff's sweep (from inside cc-reconcile), the cc-sense coherence pass and cc-bundle's tick (one worker for the queued rows that share a file, once the landing queue has room). NONE HAS A TIMER OF ITS OWN, deliberately — a watcher that runs beside the others is a fourth thing to read, so this turn carries them. cc-sense is off until `CC_SENSE=on` is in ~/.cc/config: a recurring pass over the whole box, its panes included, is the owner's call, and with no unit of its own that switch is the config key

the daily sweep: dead tracks, merged origin branches, bare windows and the worktrees dead subagents left inside the checkout (CC_JANITOR_AGENT_HOURS, default 4; 0 = off) in CC_JANITOR_REPOS (unset = no repo swept), and on every box the ccbox-* containers stopped for CC_JANITOR_CONTAINER_DAYS days or more (default 7; 0 or empty = off) — enabled everywhere because the container sweep is default-on by design: a stopped ccbox is a leftover the audit would otherwise flag forever, and a box without docker hears nothing

the 5 min host push for interactive member sessions: inside a workspace's boundary the Stop hook commits but cannot push (the credential is host-only by design), and only a worker's loop pushed from the host — two commits sat on the box for a day, 2026-09-04. Switched off, a member's work stays local until somebody pushes by hand and nothing says so: the `push!` a member project shows is THIS push's own failure record (~/.cc/push-state), not the member's own file, which no push of theirs ever clears

the secretaries — five tool-less cheap-model reads of the box every 30 min, change-gated and paced to 5 model calls an hour (120/day): measured a full tick $0.12, a quiet tick $0, so ≈$1–1.5 a normal day and ≈$3 at the cap; past the pace it judges hourly, it never stops. Same account limit the workers draw on. INSTALLED OFF: spending model budget on a watcher is the owner's call; week 1 is shadow mode (findings reach sessions, never the owner)

the drive loop — every 2 h it wakes each session so one decides whether there is work; switched off, the box does nothing until a human asks. INSTALLED OFF: the first run wakes every session on this box at once, and switching that on is the owner's call, not the installer's

the token ledger — every 5 min it folds what grew in ~/.claude/projects into ~/.cc/state/spend/ and snapshots the live claude processes, so spend is visible per session, repo, track and model and a phantom worker nobody is watching has somewhere to show up. No model call, no network. INSTALLED OFF: whether the box keeps a spend ledger at all is the owner's call
enabled even when publishing is unconfigured — it exits at once, and after a later `cc-publish setup` it must not wait for a second install
`cc slack on` owns it — it needs the tokens, so the installer never starts it
an always-on recorder is the box owner's call

daemons.why: the shell that holds a session's tmux window (`cc __run…`). One per live session, no unit owns any of them, and each ends with the session it belongs to — so the next start IS the new code, and a landing that restarted one would end the session it was launched from. Declared rather than left undeclared: without a row every landing that touches this file would name a dozen of them on the owner's card, which is how a warning stops being read

`cc-slack channel`, the per-session MCP server, one per live session and none of them a unit. Same answer and same reason as the launcher above. The Slack DAEMON is a different process and is a unit — cc-slackd.service, restarted by the step before this one
tmux-main.service's ExecStart runs this, so the units step ALREADY names a change to it as the owner's hand (`cc rc restart`) — this row exists so the same fact is not reported twice under two names

`cc-graphs serve` is started by hand from a shell, so no unit owns it and the deploy's unit steps cannot see it: PR #295 changed this file, every unit that mattered was restarted, and 127.0.0.1 kept answering from the pre-merge Python (2026-09-07). Safe to restart from a landing — loopback only, no state of its own, and `serve` is the tool's OWN restart, which stops the pid in its own pidfile rather than one a landing guessed at, and comes back on the port it was already serving
